previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a man with end-stage renal disease, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, congestive heart failure, and a history of depression and polysubstance use, was admitted for shortness of breath and chest pain after missing hemodialysis. His symptoms were attributed to fluid overload and resolved after dialysis. He reported using crack cocaine the day before admission and expressed feelings of hopelessness but denied active suicidal ideation during the stay. His mood was supported by psychiatry, and sertraline was continued. His potassium and uremic symptoms improved with dialysis, and his insulin regimen was maintained without changes due to prior hypoglycemia. He was discharged home in good condition with instructions to resume dialysis, adhere to a low-sodium diet, monitor weight, and follow up with primary care and psychiatry.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ male with chest pain.

FINDINGS:  Portable upright chest radiograph is reviewed and compared to
___.  Enlarged cardiac silhouette is unchanged.  Pulmonary vasculature is
slightly indistinct, but there is no sign of overt pulmonary edema.  Moderate
right pleural effusion has slightly increased in size since the previous exam,
and there is worsening right basilar atelectasis.  There is no definite
consolidation, although superimposed infection at the right base is difficult
to exclude.  Left lung remains clear.  There is probably a trace amount of
left pleural fluid.  There is no pneumothorax.

IMPRESSION:

1.  Worsening right pleural effusion, and atelectasis.  Superimposed infection
cannot be excluded.

2.  Probable small left pleural effusion.

INDICATION:  ___ male with increased work of breathing.  Please
evaluate for CHF.  Patient is on dialysis, and received fluids for
tachycardia.

FINDINGS:  Portable upright chest radiograph is reviewed and compared to study
from three hours prior.  Enlarged cardiac silhouette again noted.  The
pulmonary vascularity is increased slightly, with worsening perihilar haze,
and now increased interstitial opacity consistent with mild pulmonary edema. 
Bilateral pleural effusions have increased, right greater than left, as has
associated compressive bibasilar atelectasis.  Lung volumes are low, but there
is no definite superimposed consolidation.  There is no pneumothorax.

IMPRESSION:  Worsening pulmonary edema and bilateral pleural effusions, right
greater than left.

PROCEDURE:  CTA chest with and without contrast with reconstructed images on
___.

Previous CT abdomen and chest CTA examination on ___, are
available for comparison.

PROCEDURE:  Non-contrast and post-contrast examination with 100 cc of IV
Optiray were obtained from the thoracic inlet to the subdiaphragmatic region
with reformatted images in both axial and both coronal, sagittal and oblique
images.
HISTORY:  ___ man with back pain and shortness of breath.  Evaluate
for any signs of dissection or PE.

FINDINGS:

The pulmonary arteries are well opacified with contrast showing no evidence of
pulmonary embolism.  The ascending aorta, arch, and descending aorta are
normal in size with no evidence of dissection.

However, the heart size is globally enlarged, moderate to severe,increased
when compared to ___, examination.

Chronic bilateral, right much more than left, pleural effusions have slightly
worsened on today's examination (moderate-to-severe right pleural effusion and
small-to-moderate left pleural effusion).  The effusions extend into the
fissures and there is also a component of left pleural effusion along the
mediastinal reflection adjacent to the aortic arch.

Multiple subcentimeter lymph nodes are seen in both axillary regions.  No
pathologically enlarged lymph nodes are noted in the hilar or mediastinal
regions.

The pulmonary parenchyma demonstrates small septal thickening and patchy areas
of ground-glass opacities.

The airways are patent to the subsegmental level.  However, at the thoracic
portion of the trachea, there is probably an element of tracheomalacia.

The bones do not show any lesions suspicious for malignancy and/or infection.
Multiple anterior ossifications along the anterior borders of the vertebral
bodies at multiple contiguous levels are consistent with DISH.

The limited evaluation of the abdomen demonstrates no significant abnormality.

IMPRESSION:

1.  No pulmonary embolism.

2.  No examination for aortic dissection.

3.  Worsening cardiomegaly (moderate to severe).

4.  Worsening bilateral pleural effusions, right more than left.

5.  Mild pulmonary edema, most likely secondary to a cardiogenic cause.

6.  Bilateral small axillary lymph nodes.  Clinical correlation  is
recommended.

HISTORY:  ___ male with congestive heart failure, coronary artery
disease and large right-sided effusion, status post recent thoracentesis.
Evaluate for pneumothorax.

COMPARISON:  Comparison is made to portable chest radiograph from ___.

FINDINGS:  There is marked reduction in the size of the right pleural effusion
following thoracentesis.  There is, however, still a mild-to-moderate amount
of residual effusion on the right.  There is no evidence for pneumothorax. The
lungs are otherwise clear with no consolidation.  The cardiac contour is
stably large, and there is vascular prominence suggesting volume overload.
However, the pulmonary edema seen on prior film does appear to be resolving.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Marked reduction in volume of the right-sided pleural effusion following
thoracentesis.  No evidence for pneumothorax.
2.  Stable cardiomegaly with vascular prominence suggesting volume overload.
However, pulmonary edema seems to be resolving.

INDICATION:  ___ with CAD and chest pain after cocaine use.

___ chest radiograph:

SINGLE AP UPRIGHT BEDSIDE CHEST RADIOGRAPH:  Pulmonary edema has waxed and
waned.  Today, edema is improved compared to two days prior, but worsened
compared to one day prior, with slightly increased pulmonary vascular
engorgement with unchanged diffuse ground-glass opacity.  Effusions have also
increased slightly in size.  Severe cardiomegaly is stable.  No pneumothorax.

IMPRESSION:  Slightly worsened cardiopulmonary decompensation and slightly
increased size of bilateral pleural effusions.

HISTORY:  CHF, abdominal pain, and obstructive cholestasis pattern.

Comparison is made to prior ultrasound dated ___, prior CT dated
___, and prior MRI dated ___.

ABDOMINAL ULTRASOUND:  Liver parenchyma is homogenous with no focal intra-
hepatic lesions identified.  Portal vein is patent with normal hepatopetal
flow but slightly increased cardiac pulsatility transmitted through.  The
hepatic veins are again noted to be moderately distended as seen on prior
examinations, likely related to the patient's underlying right-sided heart
dysfunction.  Gallbladder is predominantly contracted but may display minimal
wall thickening even given the luminal distention.  No pericholecystic fluid
is identified, and there is no evidence of cholelithiasis.  No intra-hepatic
ductal dilatation is noted with the CHD measuring 2 mm.  The spleen is top
normal in size at 13 cm.  A mild- to-moderate amount of intra- abdominal
ascites is noted in addition to a known right pleural effusion.
Pancreas is not visualized.

IMPRESSION:

1.  No focal intra-hepatic lesions or ductal dilatation identified.  Moderate
dilatation of the hepatic veins and increased cardiac pulsatility within the
portal venous waveform likely reflect underlying right-sided heart
dysfunction.  Conjestive hepatopathy due to underlying cardiac function should
be considered.

2.  Mild gallbladder wall thickening likely related to underdistension and
mild third spacing.  Mild-to-moderate amount of intra-abdominal ascites and
right pleural effusion.

3.  Inability to visualize pancreatic lesions
